title: Why the Grand Alliance broke down
summary: The alliance against Hitler concealed rival political systems and incompatible security aims; victory removed the pressure to compromise.

sections.heading: A coalition of necessity
sections.body: The Soviet Union, Britain and the United States cooperated because defeating Nazi Germany mattered more than their disagreements. Stalin needed a western front to relieve the Red Army; Britain required American resources; Roosevelt wanted Soviet military assistance and a workable post-war international organisation. This was effective military collaboration, but it did not create a shared vision of Europe. Earlier antagonisms, including Western intervention in the Russian Civil War and the Nazi–Soviet Pact, remained part of how leaders interpreted one another.

sections.heading: From common enemy to power vacuum
sections.body: The defeat of Germany removed the central reason for cooperation. The Soviet army controlled much of eastern Europe, while American economic strength and the temporary atomic monopoly created a very different basis of power. Stalin sought friendly governments on invasion routes into the USSR; Washington associated recovery with open trade and political choice. Security for one side could therefore look like expansion to the other. Poland and Germany exposed these contradictions more sharply than abstract ideological speeches.

sections.heading: Building an argument
sections.body: Explain the sequence rather than assuming war was inevitable in 1943. Wartime negotiations and the founding of the UN demonstrate continuing cooperation. By 1947–1949, rival aid programmes, political consolidation and the Berlin confrontation had made division more durable. A strong judgement distinguishes the underlying conditions for conflict from the decisions that transformed mistrust into opposing blocs.

debate: Was breakdown primarily ideological, or a security dilemma produced by the defeat of Germany?
judgement: Ideology shaped perceptions, but the post-war power vacuum and specific choices over Germany and eastern Europe explain the timing of the breakdown.
pitfall: Do not treat the alliance as harmonious before 1945 or the Cold War as an automatic consequence of communism existing.
retrieval: What did each ally need from the coalition?
Which event changed mistrust into institutional division?
What evidence challenges inevitability?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 12–17, 30–37 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam: agreements and fault lines
summary: The conferences achieved substantial cooperation while leaving unresolved questions about sovereignty, Germany and the meaning of democracy.

sections.heading: Tehran and Yalta
sections.body: At Tehran in late 1943, military cooperation remained the priority: the western invasion of France and Soviet pressure in the east would defeat Germany. Discussion of Poland revealed Stalin’s security concerns and the importance of territorial arrangements. At Yalta in February 1945, the leaders agreed occupation arrangements for Germany, principles for liberated Europe, Soviet entry into the war against Japan and plans for the United Nations. Commitments to democratic government did not settle how free political competition would operate where Soviet troops were present.

sections.heading: Why Potsdam was different
sections.body: By Potsdam, Germany had surrendered, Roosevelt had died and Truman was president. Churchill was replaced during the conference by Attlee. These changes reduced personal continuity, but the deeper problem was that wartime priorities no longer required the same concessions. Reparations and economic recovery pulled policy in different directions. The successful American atomic test also altered the strategic context, although Stalin already knew of the project through intelligence.

sections.heading: Use in an essay
sections.body: Compare what changed and what continued across the conferences. The allies still agreed on disarmament, denazification and occupation, so Potsdam was not simply a complete diplomatic failure. Its importance lies in unresolved arrangements becoming harder to reconcile once implemented. Evaluate leaders alongside military occupation and economic interests: personnel mattered, but no change of president could remove the conflicting interests over Poland and Germany.

debate: Did Truman’s arrival cause a rupture, or reveal contradictions already present under Roosevelt?
judgement: The conferences postponed rather than resolved several conflicts; changing circumstances made ambiguous agreements increasingly unstable.
pitfall: Do not claim that Yalta simply authorised a communist Poland or that the permanent division of Germany was already a settled final objective.
retrieval: Give two agreements and one unresolved issue at Yalta.
How did the situation change before Potsdam?
Why does UN cooperation complicate an inevitable-conflict argument?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 17–29 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Ideology, fear and the security dilemma
summary: Mutual fear became dangerous because each side interpreted the other’s security policies through hostile ideological assumptions.

sections.heading: Ideological lenses
sections.body: The USSR’s Marxist-Leninist leadership viewed capitalism as hostile to socialism and was deeply suspicious of Western economic influence. American leaders associated Soviet one-party rule with expansion and the suppression of political freedom. These differences did not prevent wartime cooperation, but they shaped interpretations once the common enemy disappeared. An economic aid programme could be presented as recovery by its sponsors and as political penetration by its opponents.

sections.heading: Fear translated into policy
sections.body: Soviet wartime losses and the history of invasion gave buffer states a strong security rationale. Yet imposing obedient governments denied political choice and alarmed Western leaders. American efforts to rebuild western Europe reduced vulnerability to economic collapse, but convinced Stalin that the United States would remain permanently influential on the continent. The Long Telegram in February 1946 explained Soviet behaviour as a durable challenge; the Novikov Telegram later that year portrayed American ambitions as expansionist.

sections.heading: Avoid false symmetry
sections.body: A security-dilemma explanation does not require claiming that every action was equally defensive or equally justified. Test intentions against methods and effects. Soviet coercion in eastern Europe and American economic leverage were different forms of power. The useful analytical question is how policies intended to protect one side narrowed the options of the other and encouraged further escalation, while acknowledging local political choices.

debate: Can mutual insecurity explain conflict without excusing coercion or erasing unequal responsibility?
judgement: Fear and ideology reinforced one another: ideology supplied the language of suspicion, while concrete security disputes gave it political force.
pitfall: Do not label every Soviet action defensive or assume that the USA acted without economic and strategic interests.
retrieval: How can a defensive policy create an offensive appearance?
Compare the telegrams’ interpretations.
Which evidence would distinguish ideology from security?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 30–37, 49–51 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Truman Doctrine and the development of containment
summary: Containment began as resistance to further communist expansion, but its methods widened from economic support to major military commitments.

sections.heading: The immediate trigger
sections.body: Britain could no longer sustain assistance to Greece and Turkey in 1947. Truman presented support as a wider struggle against coercion and requested $400 million. The Greek conflict was not simply a Soviet invasion: local communists and neighbouring communist states mattered, and Stalin had largely respected Greece’s place in the British sphere. The gap between complex local politics and a universal ideological explanation is important when evaluating the doctrine.

sections.heading: Changing instruments
sections.body: Containment did not mean liberating every existing communist state. Kennan favoured patient political and economic resistance and warned against direct war with the USSR. Marshall aid, alliances and later military intervention developed alongside that approach. NSC-68 in 1950 called for a substantial build-up; the Korean War made greater spending and global military commitments politically easier. The same broad goal therefore produced different policies in different places.

sections.heading: Measure success carefully
sections.body: The survival of non-communist governments in western Europe and South Korea supports an argument for success. However, military costs, support for authoritarian allies and the tendency to misread nationalist movements as Soviet instruments qualify that claim. Establish the geographical and chronological scope of the question before judging containment. A policy can prevent expansion in one theatre while intensifying confrontation more generally.

evidence: 1947: $400 million requested for Greece and Turkey
debate: Was containment a restrained alternative to war or an expandable justification for intervention?
judgement: Containment was influential precisely because it was flexible, but that flexibility could turn limited resistance into expensive global commitments.
pitfall: Do not equate containment with rollback, or suggest that Stalin directly controlled every communist movement.
retrieval: Why did British weakness matter?
How did Korea change containment?
What criteria would you use to judge success?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 32–36, 76–83 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Marshall Plan, Cominform and economic division
summary: Economic reconstruction offered security and influence; Soviet rejection and counter-organisation helped crystallise two European blocs.

sections.heading: American purposes
sections.body: Marshall proposed European recovery assistance in June 1947. Food, fuel, industrial reconstruction and financial support helped restore confidence after wartime destruction. Economic recovery was also political: it reduced the appeal of communist parties and created stable trading partners. These purposes were compatible rather than mutually exclusive. An essay should avoid treating humanitarian assistance and American self-interest as a simple either-or choice.

sections.heading: Soviet interpretation and response
sections.body: Aid was offered beyond western Europe, but participation involved cooperation and economic information that Stalin considered threatening. He rejected it and pressured eastern European governments to do the same. Cominform, created in 1947, tightened coordination among communist parties; Comecon followed in 1949 as an economic organisation. These were not identical institutions: one concerned political organisation, the other economic cooperation under Soviet predominance.

sections.heading: Impact and limits
sections.body: American assistance accelerated recovery and linked western Europe more closely to the United States. Soviet refusal narrowed opportunities for all-European cooperation and reinforced the division of economic systems. Nevertheless, Europe’s recovery also depended on domestic reforms, labour and pre-existing industrial capacity. Treat the plan as a major catalyst and instrument of influence, rather than the sole cause of either recovery or the Cold War.

debate: Was Marshall aid primarily recovery, containment or economic expansion?
judgement: The programme combined all three; its Cold War significance came from how aid and Soviet rejection hardened opposing political-economic systems.
pitfall: Do not say that aid was originally offered only to capitalist states, or confuse Cominform with Comecon.
retrieval: Why did Stalin reject participation?
How did economic aid support containment?
Why is recovery not proof of a purely altruistic motive?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 33–37 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Sovietisation of eastern Europe
summary: Soviet military presence enabled communist consolidation, but its timing and mechanisms varied across eastern Europe.

sections.heading: Occupation and political control
sections.body: The Red Army’s advance left the USSR with decisive leverage in much of eastern Europe. Soviet security concerns encouraged friendly governments, but “friendly” increasingly meant governments unable to challenge Moscow. Communist parties gained control of key ministries, weakened rivals and narrowed political competition. Coalition arrangements could therefore become stages towards one-party rule rather than durable pluralism.

sections.heading: Variation matters
sections.body: The region was not transformed by a single identical process. Local communist strength, wartime resistance, coalition politics and Soviet pressure interacted differently. Yugoslavia’s partisans had their own power base, explaining why Tito could later resist Stalin. Czechoslovakia’s communist takeover in 1948 was especially alarming in the West because it demonstrated the fragility of coalition politics. Such variation helps prevent an essay from reducing eastern Europeans to passive objects.

sections.heading: Responsibility and consequences
sections.body: Sovietisation strengthened Stalin’s strategic buffer but undermined wartime promises about political choice and encouraged Western containment. Explain both purposes and consequences. The policy was defensive in geographical motivation but frequently coercive in implementation. By 1949, rival political and economic institutions made compromise more difficult, although the Tito–Stalin split also revealed that the communist bloc was not completely uniform.

evidence: 1945: Soviet forces dominate much of eastern Europe
debate: Does a security motive make Sovietisation defensive when its methods removed sovereignty and political competition?
judgement: Sovietisation was a major cause of Western alarm because security was pursued through political domination; local variation limits the idea of a perfectly controlled monolith.
pitfall: Do not claim that every communist government was installed by Soviet troops or became communist on the same date.
retrieval: Which mechanisms converted coalitions into one-party states?
Why is Yugoslavia a useful exception?
How did Sovietisation affect US choices?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 30–37, 54–66 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Berlin blockade and airlift
summary: The first major Berlin confrontation entrenched German division while demonstrating that determined resistance could avoid direct war.

sections.heading: Causes beyond a single trigger
sections.body: Germany’s industrial capacity and strategic position made its future central to both superpowers. Western reconstruction and the merging of occupation zones conflicted with Soviet priorities over reparations and security. Currency reform in the western zones and western sectors of Berlin sharpened the dispute in June 1948. West Berlin’s location inside the Soviet occupation zone made access vulnerable and created an opportunity to pressure the Western powers.

sections.heading: Choice of response
sections.body: The Soviet blockade cut surface access to the western sectors. The United States and Britain supplied the population by air instead of withdrawing or forcing an armed convoy through. This mattered because both sides could maintain their positions without deliberately starting a shooting war. The airlift became a demonstration of Western resolve and logistical capacity, but it was also a calculated way of limiting escalation.

sections.heading: Consequences for the Cold War
sections.body: The blockade ended in May 1949 without removing the Western presence. Separate German states emerged that year, and NATO was established during the confrontation. The crisis therefore failed to achieve Soviet pressure objectives and reinforced Western cooperation. Yet it did not cause every subsequent division on its own: plans for western German reconstruction and alliance-building predated the blockade. Distinguish acceleration from original causation.

evidence: 1949: Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic created
debate: Was the blockade an expansionist attempt to expel the West or a response to Western moves towards a separate German state?
judgement: Whatever Stalin’s motive, the outcome strengthened Western cohesion and made an already developing German division more permanent.
pitfall: Do not confuse the 1948 blockade with the 1961 Berlin Wall, or describe the airlift as an invasion.
retrieval: What made Berlin geographically vulnerable?
Why did the airlift limit escalation?
Name one immediate and one structural consequence.
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 38–45 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: NATO, Warsaw Pact and the early arms race
summary: Institutional alliances and nuclear competition turned post-war distrust into a more durable military confrontation.

sections.heading: Alliance formation
sections.body: NATO’s creation in April 1949 bound the United States and Canada more closely to western European security. It reassured vulnerable allies and signalled that American involvement would outlast reconstruction. Soviet leaders interpreted Western military cooperation and later West German rearmament as threats. The Warsaw Pact in 1955 consolidated the eastern alliance after West Germany joined NATO; it was not formed simultaneously with NATO in 1949.

sections.heading: Ending the atomic monopoly
sections.body: The Soviet atomic test in August 1949 ended the American monopoly. Both sides subsequently developed thermonuclear weapons and increasingly capable delivery systems. These developments raised the potential cost of war and encouraged deterrence, but also produced fear of falling behind. Nuclear possession should not be confused with exact numerical or technological parity: equality in every category did not suddenly appear in 1949.

sections.heading: Military strength and instability
sections.body: An arms race can stabilise relations by making direct conflict prohibitively costly, yet destabilise them by increasing secrecy, worst-case planning and crisis pressure. Korea encouraged military spending and strengthened the rationale for alliances. Use this tension to evaluate the arms race: more weapons did not simply produce more security, and avoiding superpower war did not prevent destructive fighting elsewhere.

evidence: 1952: US thermonuclear test; 1953: Soviet thermonuclear development
May 1955: West Germany joins NATO; Warsaw Pact established
debate: Did alliances and nuclear weapons deter war or institutionalise the confrontation?
judgement: They did both: military deterrence reduced incentives for direct attack while making division more durable and crises more dangerous.
pitfall: Do not treat the Warsaw Pact as a 1949 organisation or equate an atomic test with complete strategic parity.
retrieval: Why was West German rearmament contentious?
What changed in August 1949?
How can deterrence and insecurity coexist?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 38–48, 146–152 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: China’s revolution and Cold War expansion into Asia
summary: The communist victory in China transformed American perceptions, but Mao’s revolution was not simply an extension of Soviet command.

sections.heading: Domestic origins of victory
sections.body: The Chinese Civil War grew from a long struggle between the Nationalists and Chinese Communist Party. Wartime disruption, Nationalist weaknesses and communist mobilisation mattered independently of the superpowers. Soviet occupation of Manchuria and assistance affected the balance, but Mao’s movement possessed its own political and military foundations. Recognising those foundations is essential when explaining why later Sino-Soviet relations could deteriorate.

sections.heading: Superpower interpretations
sections.body: Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic in October 1949, while the Nationalists retreated to Taiwan. The United States continued to recognise the Republic of China and interpreted the mainland outcome as a major failure to contain communism. Washington often assumed greater coordination between Moscow and Beijing than actually existed. Stalin, meanwhile, was uneasy about Mao’s independence even while seeking a strategic partner.

sections.heading: Consequences
sections.body: The 1950 Sino-Soviet alliance appeared to confirm a powerful communist bloc. Combined with the Soviet atomic test and then the Korean War, it encouraged a more militarised American approach to Asia. However, the alliance contained inequalities and mistrust. Use China to challenge a purely European account of Cold War origins and to demonstrate that shared ideology did not erase national interests.

debate: Was communist victory chiefly a Soviet gain or an autonomous revolution that created a new centre of power?
judgement: It strengthened the apparent communist bloc but also introduced an independent revolutionary state whose ambitions would challenge Soviet leadership.
pitfall: Do not describe China as a Soviet satellite or claim American diplomatic recognition of the PRC followed immediately in 1949.
retrieval: Why did US interpretations exaggerate communist unity?
Which domestic factors matter?
How did 1949 change the strategic context?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 71–75, 112–118 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Korean War: containment, rollback and limits
summary: Korea transformed containment into major warfare and exposed the danger of pursuing reunification beyond a limited defensive objective.

sections.heading: From division to invasion
sections.body: Korea’s post-war division produced rival governments claiming authority over the whole peninsula. Kim Il-sung pressed for military reunification and obtained Soviet support; Mao’s position was also important. The North Korean invasion in June 1950 was therefore both a local struggle and an international crisis. It should not be explained solely as an order from Stalin or solely as a civil war isolated from Cold War politics.

sections.heading: Escalation and restraint
sections.body: US-led UN forces defended the South and reversed the invasion after the Inchon landing. Crossing the 38th parallel changed the objective from restoring South Korea to attempting reunification under its government. Chinese intervention then drove the conflict back towards stalemate. Truman’s dismissal of MacArthur in April 1951 illustrated the political determination to keep the war limited rather than attack China and risk wider confrontation.

sections.heading: Outcome and significance
sections.body: The July 1953 armistice preserved a divided peninsula near the pre-war boundary. Containment succeeded in preventing the conquest of South Korea; rollback failed and the human cost was immense. American defence spending, Asian commitments and support for West German rearmament increased. The war helped globalise and militarise the Cold War, while also demonstrating that nuclear powers could accept an unsatisfactory settlement rather than risk total war.

debate: Should the outcome be judged a successful containment operation or an expensive strategic stalemate?
judgement: It was successful against the original invasion but unsuccessful as rollback; its wider importance was the militarisation of a global Cold War.
pitfall: Do not call the armistice a peace treaty or assume the border was radically transformed.
retrieval: When did containment become rollback?
Why did China intervene?
Give two consequences beyond Korea.
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 76–83 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Khrushchev and peaceful coexistence
summary: Peaceful coexistence aimed to manage competition without world war, not to abandon ideological rivalry or Soviet control of its bloc.

sections.heading: A changed strategic calculation
sections.body: Stalin’s death in 1953 opened space for a different diplomatic style. Nuclear weapons made direct conflict increasingly dangerous, while Soviet leaders wanted resources for domestic development. Khrushchev argued that capitalist and communist states could compete without an inevitable world war. Summit diplomacy, the Austrian settlement and improved contacts demonstrated opportunities for accommodation, although Soviet leadership emerged through a succession struggle rather than an instant uncontested transfer.

sections.heading: The contradiction of reform and control
sections.body: De-Stalinisation challenged aspects of Stalin’s rule and raised expectations within the eastern bloc. Khrushchev’s 1956 Secret Speech encouraged hopes of change, but Soviet intervention in Hungary showed the limits. Reform within a secure communist sphere might be tolerated; withdrawal from the alliance and the loss of communist power were another matter. His policy therefore combined more flexible rhetoric with the preservation of essential strategic interests.

sections.heading: Evaluate through contrasting episodes
sections.body: Berlin ultimatums, the U-2 incident and Cuba demonstrate that coexistence included pressure and brinkmanship. The resolution of Cuba and the 1963 test-ban agreement show a willingness to negotiate after confrontation. Judge the policy as an attempt to regulate conflict with uneven results, rather than classifying Khrushchev simply as either a peacemaker or an aggressor.

debate: Were crises failures of coexistence or instruments within a competitive policy intended to avoid general war?
judgement: Coexistence helped establish negotiation as legitimate, but its effects were limited by alliance control, prestige and Khrushchev’s risky pressure tactics.
pitfall: Do not confuse coexistence with ideological agreement or unrestricted independence for Soviet allies.
retrieval: What did coexistence permit and exclude?
How did Hungary reveal its limits?
Which episode best supports a qualified success judgement?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 88–94, 107–128 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Hungarian uprising and Soviet intervention
summary: Hungary exposed the limits of de-Stalinisation and Western liberation rhetoric within the Soviet sphere.

sections.heading: Sources of rebellion
sections.body: Political repression, economic hardship and resentment of Soviet domination created opposition in Hungary. Khrushchev’s criticism of Stalin and developments in Poland raised expectations that change might be possible. Demonstrations in October developed into a broader challenge to the regime. Imre Nagy’s return to power and reform proposals represented an attempt to find a more independent political future rather than a simple foreign conspiracy.

sections.heading: The Soviet decision
sections.body: The movement went beyond changes of personnel. Multi-party politics, neutrality and withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact threatened Soviet alliance cohesion. Soviet forces intervened decisively in November and installed a dependable leadership under János Kádár. The distinction between reform inside the bloc and leaving the bloc helps explain why Moscow tolerated some Polish changes but used overwhelming force in Hungary.

sections.heading: International significance
sections.body: The United States did not intervene militarily despite anti-communist rhetoric. Hungary lay within the Soviet sphere, and direct intervention risked a much wider war. The simultaneous Suez crisis complicated the international setting but is not a complete explanation for Western inaction. The outcome damaged communist credibility abroad and demonstrated the practical limits of rollback. Compare it with Cuba to assess how geography and perceived vital interests shaped crisis management.

evidence: 1 November: Nagy declares neutrality and intention to leave Warsaw Pact
debate: Was intervention chiefly ideological repression or defence of a strategic sphere?
judgement: The two were closely linked: preserving communist power maintained Soviet strategic control, at the cost of legitimacy and human freedom.
pitfall: Avoid inflated casualty figures in short revision sheets; do not date the declaration of neutrality to 29 October.
retrieval: Why did reform become unacceptable to Moscow?
Why did the West not use force?
What did the crisis reveal about rollback?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 88–94 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Berlin crisis and the Wall
summary: The Wall was a humanitarian catastrophe and propaganda defeat, but also stabilised an immediate source of East-West confrontation.

sections.heading: Why Berlin remained vulnerable
sections.body: West Berlin was a Western enclave inside East Germany and a route through which East Germans could leave. The loss of skilled workers weakened the GDR and exposed its lack of popular confidence. Khrushchev sought changes to the city’s status and demanded a Western withdrawal, while East German leader Walter Ulbricht pressed for a solution to the refugee crisis. Local allies therefore influenced superpower choices.

sections.heading: Pressure and the settlement by division
sections.body: Khrushchev’s 1958 ultimatum did not produce the withdrawal he wanted. The Vienna meeting with Kennedy in 1961 failed to resolve the dispute. On 13 August, East German authorities began closing the border and constructing barriers. Kennedy defended Western access and the Western sectors but did not attempt to demolish the barrier, recognising that doing so could produce war. Later tank confrontations showed that escalation remained possible.

sections.heading: A mixed outcome
sections.body: The Wall stopped most emigration and secured the GDR’s immediate survival, while visibly contradicting claims of communist superiority. Families were divided and people seeking escape faced lethal danger. For superpower relations, the stabilisation of the boundary reduced one recurring pressure point. In an essay distinguish humanitarian consequences, propaganda outcomes and strategic effects: the same event can be a failure by one measure and a success by another.

debate: Did the Wall increase Cold War tension or contain a crisis that risked becoming worse?
judgement: It dramatised division and repression but reduced the immediate refugee problem that had destabilised the East German state.
pitfall: Do not describe the Wall as a Western construction or confuse emigration from East Germany with movement into it.
retrieval: Why did Ulbricht want border closure?
What did Kennedy defend?
How can propaganda defeat coexist with strategic stabilisation?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 107–111 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Cuba, the Bay of Pigs and the road to missiles
summary: Cuban nationalism, American pressure and Soviet opportunity interacted to turn a revolution into a superpower flashpoint.

sections.heading: A revolution with its own agenda
sections.body: Castro’s overthrow of Batista in January 1959 was rooted in Cuban politics and opposition to dictatorship, inequality and foreign influence. The new government’s reforms and nationalisation threatened American interests. Relations deteriorated through reciprocal measures: Soviet trade offered an alternative market and supplies, while American economic pressure encouraged a closer Cuban relationship with Moscow. Avoid projecting a fully settled Soviet alliance backwards onto the revolution’s beginning.

sections.heading: The Bay of Pigs
sections.body: The CIA-backed invasion by Cuban exiles in April 1961 failed to overthrow Castro. The expected internal uprising did not occur and the invaders were defeated. The operation damaged Kennedy’s prestige, strengthened Castro’s revolutionary legitimacy and made the threat of another American attack credible to Cuban leaders. It also increased the value of Soviet protection, making Cuba more receptive to military assistance.

sections.heading: Why missiles became attractive
sections.body: For Khrushchev, missiles could protect Cuba, challenge the strategic imbalance and create pressure on Washington. For Castro, the priority was the survival of the revolution. Their interests overlapped but were not identical. Establish this distinction before analysing the October crisis: Cuba was not merely a chess square, and the later exclusion of Castro from the settlement revealed limits on Cuban autonomy within the alliance.

evidence: 1960: Soviet trade relationship and accelerating nationalisation
April 1961: failed Bay of Pigs invasion
debate: Was Cuba pushed towards the USSR by US policy, or did Castro’s revolutionary aims make confrontation likely?
judgement: Both domestic transformation and external pressure mattered; the Bay of Pigs sharply increased the credibility of the invasion threat.
pitfall: Do not treat the Bay of Pigs as the missile crisis or describe Castro as a Soviet appointee.
retrieval: How did economic measures escalate the conflict?
Why did the invasion strengthen Castro?
How did Castro’s motives differ from Khrushchev’s?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 121–124 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Cuban Missile Crisis: danger, compromise and consequences
summary: The crisis combined extreme danger with negotiated restraint; the settlement was more reciprocal than the public image of an American victory suggested.

sections.heading: Escalation
sections.body: American reconnaissance identified Soviet missile installations in October 1962. Kennedy rejected immediate invasion or air strikes in favour of a naval quarantine, creating time for negotiation while demonstrating resolve. The crisis was not safely controlled at every moment: military incidents and imperfect information could have produced escalation beyond leaders’ intentions. The shooting down of a U-2 aircraft on 27 October illustrated this danger.

sections.heading: The bargain
sections.body: Khrushchev agreed to remove Soviet missiles in exchange for a public American undertaking not to invade Cuba. A private American commitment to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey also formed part of the settlement. This matters for evaluation: Kennedy’s public success depended partly on a concealed concession. Castro’s exclusion from the principal negotiations left him dissatisfied even though the non-invasion pledge helped protect his government.

sections.heading: Longer-term effects
sections.body: The crisis encouraged communication and limited arms-control measures, including the hotline agreement and the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty. It did not end the arms race or ideological competition. Khrushchev’s prestige suffered and China criticised Soviet retreat. A balanced judgement should separate the immediate removal of danger from the longer-term continuation of rivalry, and recognise both leadership restraint and the hazards those leaders had helped create.

evidence: 27 October: U-2 shot down and intensive negotiations
28 October: settlement; 1963: hotline and test-ban treaty
debate: Did firmness win the crisis, or did reciprocal compromise prevent disaster?
judgement: Firmness created bargaining pressure, but compromise and restraint were indispensable to avoiding war; a simple winner-loser account misses the private bargain.
pitfall: Do not omit the Turkish missile commitment or claim the crisis ended the Cold War.
retrieval: Why choose quarantine rather than an immediate strike?
What did each superpower concede?
Which consequence reduced future risk?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 121–126 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: The Sino-Soviet split
summary: Shared communism could not overcome rival leadership claims, national interests and disagreements over revolutionary strategy.

sections.heading: Unequal partnership
sections.body: The 1950 alliance did not erase Mao’s resentment of Soviet seniority or Stalin’s suspicion of Chinese independence. China’s costs in Korea and dependence on Soviet assistance reinforced these tensions. After Stalin’s death, hopes of better relations gave way to disagreement over Khrushchev’s de-Stalinisation and peaceful coexistence. Mao regarded Soviet accommodation with the West as a departure from revolutionary commitments and a challenge to his own style of leadership.

sections.heading: Disputes become a split
sections.body: The Taiwan Strait crises exposed differing attitudes towards nuclear risk and alliance obligations. Soviet reluctance to support every Chinese confrontation angered Beijing; Moscow resented being drawn into dangers it had not chosen. Nuclear cooperation was curtailed and Soviet advisers withdrew in 1960. Public ideological criticism in the early 1960s and border clashes in 1969 demonstrated that the dispute extended beyond personal dislike.

sections.heading: Cold War significance
sections.body: The split undermined the American assumption of a unified communist bloc and created opportunities for triangular diplomacy. China increasingly feared Soviet power, helping make rapprochement with the USA attractive. Evaluate ideology alongside sovereignty, security and status. It is misleading to call ideology a disguise with no importance, but equally misleading to ignore the strategic border and the competition to lead the communist world.

debate: Was the split ideological or a conflict of national interests?
judgement: Ideology and national interests reinforced one another: doctrinal arguments expressed genuine differences while legitimising competing claims to leadership and security.
pitfall: Do not treat the split as a single event in 1956 or assume China and the USSR remained coordinated throughout the Cold War.
retrieval: Why did Mao oppose de-Stalinisation?
How did Taiwan expose alliance tensions?
Why did the split help US diplomacy?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 112–120, 153–157 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Why détente emerged
summary: Détente was a practical attempt to manage rivalry under nuclear, economic and political constraints, rather than an end to competition.

sections.heading: Nuclear and economic incentives
sections.body: Cuba demonstrated the danger of miscalculation, while increasingly destructive arsenals made an outright strategic victory implausible. Arms expenditure competed with domestic priorities. Soviet leaders wanted access to technology and economic opportunities; American leaders faced the financial and political costs of Vietnam. These pressures encouraged negotiation, but neither side needed to abandon its system or its international interests to pursue it.

sections.heading: Diplomacy in a changing world
sections.body: The Sino-Soviet split created a three-sided relationship in which Washington could improve ties with Beijing and Moscow. European leaders also acted independently: West German Ostpolitik sought more workable relations across the division of Europe. Détente was therefore not solely a personal initiative by Nixon and Brezhnev, though their leadership helped turn favourable conditions into agreements.

sections.heading: Define success realistically
sections.body: Arms-control agreements, summits, trade and the Helsinki process improved predictability. They did not remove proxy conflict or settle every dispute over human rights and spheres of influence. Treat détente as regulated competition. A strong essay assesses whether it reduced the risk of direct war and improved communication, rather than declaring it a failure merely because rivalry continued somewhere in the world.

evidence: 1963: hotline and Partial Test Ban Treaty
1972: Nixon visits Beijing and Moscow; SALT I
debate: Was détente a response to weakness or a strategy through which leaders pursued strength?
judgement: Constraints made compromise attractive, while leaders used it to protect influence; necessity and strategic opportunity worked together.
pitfall: Do not give détente one universally agreed start date or describe it as disarmament and friendship.
retrieval: Rank three causes of détente.
What did Ostpolitik contribute?
How should success be measured?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 146–157 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
CW Revision - 1957-69.pdf, Détente section.

title: SALT, Helsinki and the limits of arms control
summary: Arms-control agreements constrained selected risks and systems, while leaving substantial scope for military competition.

sections.heading: What was actually limited
sections.body: The 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty prohibited tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater, but did not ban underground testing. The 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty addressed the spread of nuclear weapons. SALT I in 1972 included an interim agreement on strategic launchers and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. These were distinct arrangements with different purposes; none amounted to the abolition of nuclear arsenals.

sections.heading: Achievement and loopholes
sections.body: Limits and verification procedures made competition more predictable and signalled that negotiated restraint was possible. However, qualitative improvements and multiple-warhead technology allowed destructive capacity to grow even when some launchers were restricted. Critics therefore argued that arms control could legitimise the arms race. Supporters countered that unmanaged competition would be more dangerous and expensive.

sections.heading: Helsinki and SALT II
sections.body: The 1975 Helsinki Final Act combined principles concerning European security, cooperation and human rights. Soviet leaders valued the recognition of the post-war European order; dissidents later used the human-rights commitments to challenge their governments. SALT II was signed in 1979 but not ratified by the US Senate. Evaluate each agreement against its actual terms rather than treating signing, ratification and implementation as interchangeable.

debate: Did arms control genuinely restrain rivalry or merely make it more manageable?
judgement: Its strongest achievement was risk management and predictability, though Helsinki also created language that strengthened later challenges to Soviet-bloc legitimacy.
pitfall: Do not claim SALT I reduced every category of nuclear weapon or that SALT II was ratified.
retrieval: What did the 1963 treaty leave permitted?
Why could arsenals become more destructive under launcher limits?
How did dissidents use Helsinki?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 146–152, 189–190 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Sino-American rapprochement and triangular diplomacy
summary: Anxiety about the USSR allowed ideological enemies to cooperate, reshaping the balance of Cold War diplomacy.

sections.heading: Why both sides reconsidered
sections.body: By the late 1960s, China regarded the Soviet Union as a serious security threat, especially after border clashes. The United States wanted leverage over Moscow, a changed diplomatic environment around Vietnam and a more flexible Asian policy. Their relationship could improve without agreement on communism or the future of Taiwan. Strategic interest made negotiation possible where ideological hostility had previously dominated.

sections.heading: The opening
sections.body: Ping-pong diplomacy and Kissinger’s secret visit in 1971 prepared the way for Nixon’s visit in February 1972. The Shanghai Communiqué set out areas of agreement and disagreement rather than creating a simple alliance. Nixon’s anti-communist credentials helped him defend a move that might have been politically more difficult for another president. Formal diplomatic recognition of the PRC came in 1979, not during the initial visit.

sections.heading: Impact and constraints
sections.body: Rapprochement increased Soviet incentives to engage Washington and confirmed that the Cold War was no longer neatly bipolar. China gained international standing and a counterweight to Moscow; the USA gained diplomatic flexibility. Taiwan remained contentious, and domestic upheavals limited the pace of change. Assess the opening as a major strategic realignment, not proof that ideological conflict had disappeared or that the USA could dictate Chinese policy.

evidence: February 1972: Nixon visit and Shanghai Communiqué
debate: Was rapprochement driven more by Nixon’s diplomatic initiative or the shared Soviet threat?
judgement: The Soviet threat created the opportunity; leadership and diplomatic preparation converted it into a durable change in relations.
pitfall: Do not call the 1972 visit full diplomatic recognition or present China as an American ally under US control.
retrieval: Why did ideological hostility become less decisive?
How did the opening affect Moscow?
What remained unresolved?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 153–157, 171 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Prague Spring and the Brezhnev Doctrine
summary: The suppression of reform in Czechoslovakia demonstrated that détente abroad could coexist with coercive control inside the Soviet bloc.

sections.heading: Reform from within
sections.body: Alexander Dubček’s leadership promoted a more open form of socialism, including reduced censorship and greater space for public debate. This was initially an attempt to reform communist rule, not simply abandon socialism for capitalism. Yet greater freedom created pressures that Soviet leaders and neighbouring hardliners feared could spread. The example was threatening precisely because it offered an alternative within the communist world.

sections.heading: Intervention and justification
sections.body: Warsaw Pact forces invaded in August 1968 and reversed the reform process. The principle later called the Brezhnev Doctrine asserted that a threat to socialism in one socialist state concerned the wider bloc. This subordinated national sovereignty to the preservation of communist power. It also exposed an enduring contradiction between claims of international equality and Soviet dominance.

sections.heading: Significance beyond Prague
sections.body: Western condemnation did not lead to military intervention. As in Hungary, the risk of superpower war and the accepted division of Europe constrained responses. The invasion weakened the appeal of Soviet communism and alarmed China, which feared similar justifications might be used against it. At the same time, superpower arms talks continued. Use the episode to show that détente was compatible with severe repression and unresolved ideological antagonism.

debate: Did intervention demonstrate Soviet strength or insecurity about the durability of communist rule?
judgement: It demonstrated military dominance but also an inability to tolerate reform without fearing the loss of control.
pitfall: Do not describe the Prague Spring as a Western invasion or equate Dubček’s initial programme with immediate NATO membership.
retrieval: Why was reform socialism threatening?
How did the doctrine restrict sovereignty?
Why did détente continue?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 141–145, 153, 189–190 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Vietnam and the limits of containment
summary: Vietnam shows how decolonisation and nationalism became entangled with global ideological competition, at enormous human cost.

sections.heading: Local roots and international support
sections.body: Vietnamese resistance developed against colonial rule and Japanese occupation, and Ho Chi Minh connected independence with communist organisation. French efforts to restore control and the subsequent division of Vietnam created a prolonged conflict over political authority. American leaders increasingly viewed the struggle through containment and the domino theory; communist powers supplied assistance to their Vietnamese partners. Vietnamese objectives were not reducible to instructions from Moscow or Beijing.

sections.heading: Escalation and American limits
sections.body: The United States escalated its direct involvement in the 1960s to preserve a non-communist South Vietnam and its credibility. Superior firepower did not solve problems of political legitimacy, rural support and the enemy’s willingness to continue fighting. The Tet Offensive in 1968 damaged confidence in optimistic American claims, even though communist forces suffered major losses. Military outcomes and political effects therefore need separate evaluation.

sections.heading: Consequences
sections.body: The United States withdrew combat forces after the 1973 Paris agreement; communist victory and reunification followed in 1975. Vietnam suffered massive destruction, displacement and social disruption. For the USA, the war exposed the limits of intervention, strained domestic politics and encouraged a more flexible diplomatic strategy. For an impact-on-countries question, prioritise Vietnamese experiences rather than writing an essay entirely about American presidential decisions.

evidence: 1954: French defeat at Dien Bien Phu and Geneva settlement
debate: Was the war principally a Cold War conflict or a struggle for national independence and reunification?
judgement: It was both; superpower intervention transformed the scale and duration of a conflict with deep local roots.
pitfall: Do not assume communist Vietnam was a passive Soviet instrument or equate a battlefield loss with political failure automatically.
retrieval: How did containment affect decolonisation?
Why was Tet politically significant?
Identify political, economic and social consequences for Vietnam.
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 172–185 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: A Soviet intervention intended to preserve a vulnerable client became a prolonged war and a major blow to détente.

sections.heading: Why Moscow intervened
sections.body: The Afghan communist government faced internal divisions, violent opposition and limited control over society. Soviet leaders feared the collapse of an allied regime on their southern border and distrusted its leadership. They interpreted intervention as protecting an existing position, but the use of force and removal of Amin appeared internationally as expansion. This gap between Soviet explanation and outside perception is central to analysing the crisis.

sections.heading: War and international reaction
sections.body: Soviet troops entered in December 1979 and installed Babrak Karmal. Resistance survived through local support, difficult terrain and assistance from outside Afghanistan, including support channelled through Pakistan. Carter responded with sanctions and the US boycott of the Moscow Olympics; SALT II ratification was shelved. Under Reagan, assistance to anti-Soviet forces intensified. A short stabilising operation became a costly and demoralising counter-insurgency.

sections.heading: Withdrawal and significance
sections.body: Gorbachev sought an exit as part of changing foreign-policy priorities. Soviet withdrawal was completed in February 1989. The war damaged prestige, consumed resources and exposed the limits of military power, but it did not single-handedly cause the USSR’s collapse. Distinguish the end of Soviet occupation from the end of Afghanistan’s conflict: the fighting continued and the Soviet-backed government survived beyond the withdrawal.

debate: Was the invasion evidence of aggressive expansion or a defensive intervention that became disastrous?
judgement: Soviet leaders sought to protect influence, but their coercive method intensified international conflict and generated costs far beyond their expectations.
pitfall: Do not claim the Afghan government fell immediately in February 1989 or that withdrawal brought peace.
retrieval: Why did Moscow distrust Amin?
How did intervention affect détente?
Why is Afghanistan insufficient as a single explanation for Soviet collapse?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 163–169, 200 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
CW Revision - 1979-91.pdf, Afghanistan and renewed tension sections.

title: Renewed confrontation and the 1983 war scare
summary: The breakdown of détente and renewed military pressure made misperception especially dangerous in the early 1980s.

sections.heading: Détente under strain
sections.body: Arms competition, disputes over human rights and interventions in the developing world undermined confidence before Afghanistan. The Soviet invasion then became a powerful symbol of confrontation. NATO’s missile decisions and Soviet deployments heightened European anxieties, while the succession of ageing Soviet leaders reduced continuity and flexibility. It is therefore misleading to make Reagan’s election the sole starting point of renewed tension.

sections.heading: Reagan and Soviet perceptions
sections.body: Reagan increased defence spending and used forceful anti-Soviet rhetoric. The Strategic Defense Initiative raised Soviet fears that an American technological breakthrough could weaken deterrence. Washington often saw its own actions as defensive or bargaining instruments; Soviet leaders could interpret them as preparations for a first strike. The danger lay in the difference between what each side intended and what the other believed.

sections.heading: Able Archer
sections.body: The NATO exercise Able Archer in November 1983 occurred in this atmosphere of suspicion. Elements of the Soviet leadership feared that an exercise might conceal real attack preparations. Its significance is not that nuclear war was certain, but that routine military activity could be read through a framework of worst-case assumptions. The episode supports an argument for the importance of communication, intelligence and empathy in later diplomacy.

evidence: September 1983: Soviet forces shoot down KAL 007
debate: Did military pressure create the conditions for later agreement or bring the superpowers dangerously close to unintended conflict?
judgement: Pressure may have increased bargaining incentives, but the war scare reveals that it also intensified insecurity and the risk of miscalculation.
pitfall: Do not describe Able Archer as a real NATO attack or claim with certainty that a launch was imminent.
retrieval: What weakened détente before Reagan?
Why could SDI alarm Moscow?
What does Able Archer reveal about perceptions?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 194–196, 163–169 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Reagan: pressure, negotiation and the end of the Cold War
summary: Reagan’s contribution requires analysing both military pressure and his later willingness to negotiate with Gorbachev.

sections.heading: The pressure argument
sections.body: Higher defence spending, support for anti-communist forces and the Strategic Defense Initiative challenged Soviet resources and confidence. Advocates of the pressure explanation argue that Moscow could not afford to compete indefinitely and therefore accepted change. This argument is strongest when linked to pre-existing Soviet economic difficulties, rather than claiming that one American programme suddenly bankrupted an otherwise healthy system.

sections.heading: The diplomatic turn
sections.body: Reagan also wanted to reduce the nuclear danger. After Gorbachev came to power, the two leaders developed a negotiating relationship through Geneva, Reykjavik and subsequent summits. The INF Treaty in 1987 eliminated an entire category of ground-launched intermediate-range missiles. This was more than an extension of rhetoric: reciprocal concessions and verification were needed to turn opportunities into an agreement.

sections.heading: Relative importance
sections.body: Reagan could influence the Soviet environment but could not dictate Gorbachev’s reforms or the decisions of eastern European populations. Conversely, Soviet change alone did not guarantee successful negotiation if Washington refused to respond. A persuasive judgement treats leadership as interaction: pressure mattered, but so did Reagan’s ability to move beyond confrontation when a reforming Soviet partner became available.

debate: Did Reagan win through pressure, or did his willingness to compromise matter more?
judgement: His most durable contribution was combining leverage with negotiated accommodation; pressure alone does not explain the peaceful character of the ending.
pitfall: Do not present Reagan as president when the USSR dissolved in 1991; George H. W. Bush succeeded him in January 1989.
retrieval: What evidence supports the pressure thesis?
What changed after 1985?
Why is negotiation not simply surrender?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 194–201, 213 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Gorbachev’s reforms and new thinking
summary: Gorbachev tried to rescue socialism, but reform and a changed foreign policy undermined mechanisms that had sustained Soviet power.

sections.heading: Domestic objectives
sections.body: Perestroika sought to restructure an inefficient economy; glasnost widened public discussion and exposed failures previously concealed. Gorbachev did not enter office with a plan to abolish the USSR or establish Western capitalism. He wanted a more effective socialist system. However, partial reforms disrupted established controls without quickly creating a stable alternative, while openness weakened official credibility and allowed grievances to circulate.

sections.heading: Changing security policy
sections.body: New thinking treated security as mutual rather than a contest that could be won through unlimited military competition. Arms agreements, withdrawal from Afghanistan and reduced coercion towards eastern Europe reflected this shift. The decision not to use Soviet force to preserve allied communist governments was especially important: opposition movements could act in circumstances very different from Hungary in 1956 or Czechoslovakia in 1968.

sections.heading: Intentions and unintended consequences
sections.body: The reforms enabled criticism of the party, revival of nationalist demands and new competition for power. Gorbachev’s choices were crucial, but their consequences depended on economic pressures, local movements and rival leaders such as Yeltsin. Separate intention from outcome and the ending of international confrontation from the collapse of the Soviet state. Neither result was simply the policy he originally designed.

evidence: 1986: Chernobyl exposes secrecy and institutional failure
debate: Was Gorbachev the decisive cause of change or the leader forced to respond to an unsustainable system?
judgement: Structural pressures made reform urgent, but his distinctive choices explain why Soviet retreat and political opening took the form they did.
pitfall: Do not define glasnost as economic restructuring or claim Gorbachev intended the USSR’s dissolution from the outset.
retrieval: Distinguish glasnost from perestroika.
Why did non-intervention matter?
How can reform undermine the system it aims to save?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 197–213 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Dissent, Solidarity and human rights
summary: Organised dissent challenged communist legitimacy from below and gave international human-rights commitments practical political force.

sections.heading: Beyond superpower leaders
sections.body: Opposition in eastern Europe grew from workplace grievances, religious networks, intellectual criticism and resentment of limited freedoms. The Helsinki commitments created a language through which activists could demand that governments follow principles they had publicly accepted. Charter 77 in Czechoslovakia exemplified this approach. These movements did not require a single Western command structure to challenge Soviet-aligned regimes.

sections.heading: Solidarity in Poland
sections.body: Workers’ strikes in 1980 produced an independent trade-union movement led by Lech Wałęsa. Solidarity linked material grievances to demands for representation and attracted support beyond a narrow workforce. The Catholic Church offered an important alternative social institution. Martial law in December 1981 suppressed open activity but failed to remove the underlying networks and dissatisfaction. Repression bought time without solving the legitimacy problem.

sections.heading: Why the late 1980s were different
sections.body: Economic weakness continued, while Gorbachev’s reforms and reduced willingness to intervene changed the risks facing opposition and governments. Negotiation became more plausible than indefinite repression. Use dissent to correct an exclusively top-down explanation of 1989: superpower choices opened opportunities, but organised local actors had to exploit them. The balance between pressure from below and permission from above varied by country.

evidence: December 1981: martial law in Poland; 1989: negotiated elections
debate: Did communist rule collapse because Moscow withdrew support, or because opposition had made it ungovernable?
judgement: Local dissent eroded legitimacy over time; Soviet non-intervention allowed that pressure to produce regime change without the previous military response.
pitfall: Do not place Charter 77 in Hungary; it was a Czechoslovak movement.
retrieval: How did Helsinki help dissidents?
Why did martial law fail to remove opposition?
What changed after Gorbachev took power?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 189–193, 203–205 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Eastern European revolutions and the fall of the Wall
summary: The collapse of communist governments was driven by local pressures within a transformed Soviet security environment.

sections.heading: A chain of opportunities
sections.body: Poland’s negotiated transition and Hungary’s reforms demonstrated alternatives to one-party rule. Openings along borders enabled East Germans to leave, weakening the GDR and encouraging protests. Mass mobilisation and the inability of governments to rely on automatic Soviet military support changed the balance. Developments in one state influenced expectations elsewhere, but the sequence was not a single plan directed from Moscow or Washington.

sections.heading: Berlin and different national paths
sections.body: The opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November became the most powerful symbol of change. It reflected sustained pressure as well as immediate administrative confusion. Other countries followed distinct paths: negotiated change in some, mass protest and elite collapse in others, and violence in Romania. These differences matter when evaluating whether 1989 was a uniformly peaceful revolution or a straightforward result of one leader’s policy.

sections.heading: Cold War consequences
sections.body: Communist monopoly and Soviet domination of eastern Europe collapsed, and German reunification followed in 1990. These developments removed a central arena of the Cold War, but the Soviet Union itself still existed. A well-structured essay can use 1989 as the decisive end of European bloc confrontation while recognising that institutional and state changes continued through 1991.

debate: How far was 1989 made possible by Gorbachev rather than caused by him?
judgement: His non-intervention was an enabling condition; local mobilisation, economic failure and national political decisions determined the actual transitions.
pitfall: Do not say the USSR dissolved when the Berlin Wall opened, or that every 1989 transition was non-violent.
retrieval: How did Hungary affect East Germany?
Why did events spread across borders?
Distinguish 1989 from 1991.
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 203–210 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Economic weakness, nationalism and Soviet collapse
summary: The USSR’s dissolution resulted from interacting economic, political and national crises; it was not simply a final military defeat by the USA.

sections.heading: Long-term weaknesses
sections.body: Low productivity, shortages and the burdens of military expenditure undermined confidence in the Soviet system. Central planning struggled to adapt, while commitments to allies and competition with the West added pressure. These weaknesses help explain why reform became urgent, but states can survive economic stagnation for long periods. Economic problems alone do not explain the timing or political form of the collapse.

sections.heading: Reform and the national question
sections.body: Greater openness weakened censorship and encouraged republics to challenge the authority of the centre. National movements drew on historical grievances and demands for self-government. Political liberalisation also created rivals within the Soviet system, including Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev increasingly faced pressure from conservatives who opposed reform and forces seeking to move further and faster than he intended.

sections.heading: The decisive breakdown
sections.body: The failed coup of August 1991 discredited hardliners and accelerated the loss of central authority. Republican independence and agreements among republican leaders then dismantled the union. Gorbachev resigned in December. Distinguish this state collapse from the earlier easing of superpower hostility and the 1989 revolutions: related processes had different actors, mechanisms and turning points.

evidence: December 1991: dissolution of the Soviet Union
debate: Were structural economic weaknesses more important than Gorbachev’s political reforms?
judgement: Economic weakness created vulnerability; reforms and nationalist mobilisation transformed vulnerability into a crisis of state authority, accelerated by the failed coup.
pitfall: Do not use “Russia” and “USSR” interchangeably or claim Reagan directly ordered the Soviet collapse.
retrieval: Why is economic weakness insufficient alone?
How did the coup affect central authority?
Separate three meanings of “the end of the Cold War”.
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 197–213 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
CW Revision - 1979-91.pdf, end-of-Cold-War sections.

title: Historiography: responsibility and changing evidence
summary: Historical interpretations are arguments to test against evidence, not labels to insert as substitutes for analysis.

sections.heading: Explaining origins
sections.body: An orthodox interpretation places substantial responsibility on Soviet expansion and coercion in eastern Europe. Revisionist approaches draw attention to American economic interests, atomic power and efforts to shape the post-war order. Post-revisionist approaches emphasise interacting security concerns, misperceptions and the structure of a divided post-war world. These categories are broad tendencies, not identical opinions held by every historian placed within them.

sections.heading: Evidence changes the debate
sections.body: Access to Soviet and other archives made it easier to examine motives and disagreements hidden by contemporary propaganda. Local and regional studies also challenged the assumption that all conflict was directed by Washington or Moscow. The Korean War and the Sino-Soviet split are useful examples: communist governments had independent aims, and shared ideology did not guarantee coordination. A richer interpretation can recognise both superpower influence and local agency.

sections.heading: Applying rather than name-dropping
sections.body: Select a claim, connect it to specific evidence and explain its limits. For instance, Stalin’s fear of invasion supports a security interpretation, but political coercion in Poland complicates a purely defensive account. The Marshall Plan supports recovery and economic-influence explanations simultaneously. You do not need invented quotations or a historian in every paragraph: what matters is evaluating plausible interpretations while maintaining your own consistent answer.

evidence: Sovietisation: useful for testing expansionist explanations
Marshall Plan: recovery and economic influence
Korea: local initiative alongside Soviet support
Sino-Soviet split: limits of ideological unity
debate: Can one school explain every phase, region and actor of the Cold War?
judgement: No single label is adequate: weigh competing explanations against the precise question, dates and evidence rather than declaring a universal winner.
pitfall: Do not invent quotations, assume every historian’s view fits one label, or make “both sides” a substitute for judgement.
retrieval: What evidence strengthens an orthodox interpretation?
How can the same policy support competing explanations?
Why do archives and local perspectives change conclusions?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 4–6, 49–51, 78–83, 112–118 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
The Paper 2 Bible.pdf, p. 3, Historiography section.

title: Comparing crises: Berlin and Cuba
summary: Compare crises through shared analytical themes: causes, methods, escalation, resolution and consequences.

sections.heading: Construct a valid comparison
sections.body: Berlin and Cuba provide examples from different regions, but define which Berlin crisis you are using. The 1948–1949 blockade and the 1958–1961 confrontation have different causes and outcomes. A comparative paragraph should make a common claim, support it from each crisis and explain the difference. Two separate narratives with a final sentence saying “both were tense” do not amount to sustained comparison.

sections.heading: Similarity: security and credibility
sections.body: In Berlin, the superpowers sought to protect their positions in divided Germany; in Cuba, Soviet and Cuban security objectives collided with American fears near its territory. Both involved prestige, local allies and the danger of a wider war. However, missiles in Cuba created a compressed nuclear confrontation, whereas Berlin involved occupation rights, access and—in 1961—emigration. Those differences shaped the available responses.

sections.heading: Difference: mechanisms and outcomes
sections.body: The airlift resisted pressure without forcing a land confrontation; the Wall stabilised the GDR through division; Cuba ended through reciprocal concessions. All demonstrate limits on leaders’ willingness to fight, but their longer-term effects differed. The blockade entrenched opposing blocs, while Cuba encouraged communication and limited arms control. Your conclusion should identify which similarity matters most and which difference best explains the contrasting outcomes.

evidence: Cuba aftermath: hotline and test-ban agreement in 1963
debate: Were Cold War crises primarily instruments of pressure or dangerous failures of mutual understanding?
judgement: They were deliberate pressure tactics with unintended risks; outcomes depended on whether leaders could defend essential interests while allowing an acceptable retreat.
pitfall: Do not combine every Berlin event into one undefined crisis or overlook a different-regions instruction.
retrieval: Write a comparative topic sentence about causes.
Which case most clearly shows compromise?
How did the crises have different long-term effects?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 38–45, 107–126 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
Cold War Past Paper Questions.docx, Question type 4: Crises.

title: Comparing leaders: Truman/Stalin and Reagan/Gorbachev
summary: Leadership comparisons need shared criteria and a clear distinction between individual choices and the circumstances leaders inherited.

sections.heading: Truman and Stalin
sections.body: For origins, compare their security aims, interpretations of the other side and policy instruments. Truman used aid, containment and alliances; Stalin consolidated friendly or dependent governments and resisted Western economic penetration. Their actions interacted rather than operating in isolation. A balanced comparison acknowledges Soviet wartime devastation and American economic strength without treating these contexts as automatic justifications for every policy.

sections.heading: Reagan and Gorbachev
sections.body: For the end, contrast Reagan’s initial pressure and later negotiation with Gorbachev’s domestic reforms and abandonment of coercive bloc maintenance. Both contributed to improved relations, but they had different resources and different abilities to transform the system. Gorbachev’s choices directly altered Soviet control over eastern Europe; Reagan’s diplomatic response helped convert Soviet change into reciprocal agreements.

sections.heading: How to judge significance
sections.body: Ask whether a leader’s policy altered the timing, direction or peacefulness of change. Separate intention from result and avoid attributing events after a leader left office directly to their personal decision. The strongest comparison weighs agency against structure: economic weakness and nuclear danger constrained choices, but leaders could still respond with repression, confrontation or compromise.

debate: Were leaders decisive, or did they mainly express structural pressures?
judgement: Leaders rarely created the underlying conditions alone, but their decisions shaped escalation, compromise and the willingness to use force.
pitfall: Do not compare two leaders from the same IB region when the question explicitly requires different regions.
retrieval: Give a shared criterion for comparing Truman and Stalin.
Why was Gorbachev’s non-intervention distinctive?
How would you test whether a leader was decisive?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 53, 194–213 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).
Cold War Past Paper Questions.docx, Question type 3: Leaders.

title: Impact on countries: Cuba and Vietnam
summary: Cuba and Vietnam show how smaller states gained support and opportunities while bearing severe costs from Cold War competition.

sections.heading: Political and security effects
sections.body: Cuba’s conflict with the USA encouraged Soviet alignment and gave Castro external protection, while exposing the limits of autonomy during the missile-crisis settlement. In Vietnam, foreign support enabled prolonged warfare and competing state-building projects. Neither country was merely passive: local leaders pursued revolutionary and national aims. Compare how external rivalry strengthened rulers, prolonged conflicts or restricted choices rather than assuming every effect was imposed from abroad.

sections.heading: Economic and social effects
sections.body: Cuba gained Soviet trade and assistance but became vulnerable to dependence on its patron, while American restrictions narrowed economic options. Vietnam endured destruction, displacement and the disruption of rural life during prolonged war. Reconstruction was shaped by the victorious government’s policies and international relationships. Keep Cold War effects separate from outcomes caused primarily by domestic policy, explaining where the two interacted.

sections.heading: A balanced comparative judgement
sections.body: The Cold War offered resources and diplomatic leverage to both states, but the benefits were uneven and accompanied by major constraints. Cuba’s survival as a revolutionary government contrasts with Vietnam’s prolonged struggle for reunification. A thematic structure—politics, economy, society—allows a direct comparison. If asked for cultural impacts, prepare specific cultural evidence rather than substituting military events or general assertions about propaganda.

evidence: Cuba: Bay of Pigs 1961 and missile crisis 1962
Vietnam: reunification after communist victory in 1975
debate: Did smaller states mainly suffer from superpower rivalry, or successfully use it for their own objectives?
judgement: Local leaders could exploit rivalry, but agency did not remove dependence, war damage or constraints on sovereignty.
pitfall: Do not answer an impact-on-countries question exclusively through US and Soviet diplomatic history, or invent cultural evidence.
retrieval: Give one political benefit and one constraint for Cuba.
Which effects in Vietnam were specifically intensified by foreign intervention?
How would a cultural-impact essay differ from a political one?
sources: Mamaux, The Cold War (Oxford, 2015), printed pp. 121–126, 172–185 (PDF pages are printed page + 6).

title: Lenin: from state breakdown to the October seizure of power
summary: War created the opportunity for revolution; Lenin’s political direction and Bolshevik organisation helped turn that opportunity into a seizure of government.

sections.heading: Conditions and opportunity
sections.body: Russia’s revolutionary crisis grew from the interaction of political weakness, social inequality and the pressures of the First World War. The fall of the tsar did not immediately produce Bolshevik rule: a Provisional Government existed alongside influential soviets. This distinction matters because explaining the collapse of the old regime is different from explaining why Lenin’s party eventually benefited. Continued war and unresolved land and economic problems undermined confidence in the new authorities.

sections.heading: Lenin’s intervention
sections.body: In the April Theses, Lenin rejected support for the Provisional Government, called for political power to pass to the soviets and proposed confiscation of landed estates. He acknowledged that the Bolsheviks were still a minority in many soviets. This is useful evidence against a narrative in which his eventual victory was inevitable. His programme combined ideological ambition with demands that could appeal to soldiers, workers and peasants facing immediate crises.

sections.heading: From mobilisation to control
sections.body: The Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd in October 1917 by the Russian calendar, November by the Gregorian calendar. Lenin provided strategic pressure for revolution, while party organisers and armed supporters were necessary to carry it out. However, taking the capital did not automatically establish control over Russia: civil war and the suppression of rivals formed a separate consolidation phase. An emergence essay should weigh the failures of opponents against the leadership and organisation that exploited them.

evidence: April 1917: Lenin’s April Theses rejected support for the Provisional Government.
The textbook identifies tsarist problems, the First World War, revolution and civil war as the foundations of the Soviet one-party state.
debate: How much explanatory weight belongs to revolutionary leadership, and how much to the collapse of alternatives?
judgement: Lenin’s intervention was a catalyst within a wider crisis; it did not create the entire crisis or guarantee nationwide control.
